text.p: The management of Kloeckner-Humboldt-Deutz AG (KHD) strove on Tuesday to convince sceptical shareholders at its annual general meeting that the troubled engine maker is on its way to a brighter future.

Management board chairman Anton Schneider said the one billion mark bank bail-out that saved the KHD from bankruptcy in June had enabled it to reduce its debt to 660 million marks at end-August from 1.547 billion marks at the end of 1994.
Sales in 1996 should equal last year's, and KHD aims to break even after posting a 1.134 billion mark net loss in 1995.
"The future of your company begins today," Schneider told shareholders repeatedly.

But angry shareholders pressed management to take responsibility for the massive losses on three cement plants in Saudi Arabia that brought the company to the brink of collapse this year for the third time in a decade.
"We must ask what is going on here," said one of the representatives of small shareholders.
Another said, "What should we be thanking these directors for, for driving the company into the wall? We should be more honest with one another. We should be able to fire these people."
But it appeared that such shareholder anger would have no direct consequences for the management.

Schneider and other holding company managers insisted that they and the company's outside auditors were deceived by the management of subsidiary Humboldt Wedag AG, and first learned of the irregularities in May.
Fifteen Wedag executives are under criminal investigation.
"The supervisory board can only review what is given to it to review, and never had the chance to uncover the manipulations at Wedag," supervisory board chairman Michael Endres said.
KHD has not yet found a buyer for the money-losing plant-construction division that it hopes to spin off, and may have to begin selling it off piecemeal, Schneider said.
But the outlook also appears difficult for Deutz AG, the restructured company that will remain after the plant division is sold.
KHD's loss on ordinary business excluding plants was 227 million marks in 1995, primarily from the engines division that will be its core business in the future.
KHD shares were trading on Tuesday at 7.80 marks, up from a traded low of 5.20 marks in June, but still down from 8.79 marks at the end of 1995.
